nodes.name: odd power sums vanish on $\chi_\lambda$
nodes.statement: For all $\lambda$ strict and $n,m \in \mathbb{N}$, $$\chi_\lambda(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^{2m+1} )= 0.$$
assumptions: For all $\lambda$ strict and $n,m \in \mathbb{N}$

nodes.name: reduction of Theorem to length-one partitions
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{action2} implies Theorem \ref{action}, that is, it is enough to show the result on modules corresponding to the partition of length one.
assumptions: Theorem \ref{action2}
conclusions: implies Theorem \ref{action}, that is, it is enough to show the result on modules corresponding to the partition of length one

nodes.name: action of $P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m}$ in terms of contents
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda = (\lambda_1,..,\lambda_n) \Vdash n$ be a shifted partition, with associated shifted Young diagram $\lambda = \{(i,j) : i = 1,..,l(\lambda) \text{ and } j = i -1 ,\ldots ,i -1+ \lambda_i. \}$. Then $$\sigma_\lambda(P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m}) =\sigma_\lambda(\sum_{i=1}^n (2M_i)^{2m}) = \sum_{i=1}^n (cont(i))^m(cont(i)+1)^m.$$
nodes.statement_short: $P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m}$ acts on $V_\lambda$ by $\sum_i (\cont(i))^m(\cont(i)+1)^m$.
assumptions: Let $\lambda = (\lambda_1,..,\lambda_n) \Vdash n$ be a shifted partition, with associated shifted Young diagram $\lambda = \{(i,j) : i = 1,..,l(\lambda) \text{ and } j = i -1 ,\ldots ,i -1+ \lambda_i. \}$

nodes.name: action of $\sum (2x_i)^{2m}$ on a length-one central character
nodes.statement: Fix a $t \in \mathbb{Z}$ Let $\mu = (\mu_1)= (t) = \Vdash t$. Then $$\chi_\mu (\sum_{i=1}^t (2x_i)^{2m} ) = \sum_{i=1}^{t} (2(i-1)-(t-1))^{2m}.$$
assumptions: Fix a $t \in \mathbb{Z}$ Let $\mu = (\mu_1)= (t) = \Vdash t$

nodes.name: super formulation of the Dirac index, $I_\#(X) = X \otimes \mathcal{S}$
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an $\mathbb{H}_\#$-supermodule, concentrated in degree zero, and $\mathcal{S}$ be a $C(V)$-supermodule.Then $I_\#(X)$ is a $\tilde{W}_\#$-supermodule and in the Grothendieck group, $$I_\#(X) = X \otimes \mathcal{S}.$$
nodes.statement_short: In the super setting the Dirac index is simply $X\otimes\mathcal{S}$, with no need to restrict $\tilde{W}_\#$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be an $\mathbb{H}_\#$-supermodule, concentrated in degree zero, and $\mathcal{S}$ be a $C(V)$-supermodule

nodes.name: $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ is an irreducible supermodule of type M or Q
nodes.statement: For a strict partition $\lambda$, when one lets $\mathcal{S}$ be a super simple spinor module, $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ is always an irreducible $\tilde{S}_n$-supermodule. If $n-l(\lambda)$ is even then $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ is type M and if $n-l(\lambda)$ is odd then $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ if of type Q.
nodes.statement_short: In the super theory $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ is always irreducible, of type M or Q according to the parity of $n-l(\lambda)$.
assumptions: For a strict partition $\lambda$, when one lets $\mathcal{S}$ be a super simple spinor module
conclusions: If $n-l(\lambda)$ is even then $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ is type M and if $n-l(\lambda)$ is odd then $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ if of type Q

nodes.name: $\Omega_\mathbb{H}\otimes 1= \rho(\Omega_{\tilde{W}})$ on Dirac cohomology
nodes.statement: On the Dirac cohomology (resp. extended Dirac index), or any submodule found inside it, namely $V_\lambda$ (resp. $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$), $$\Omega_\mathbb{H}\otimes 1= \rho(\Omega_{\tilde{W}}).$$
nodes.statement_short: The two Casimirs agree on Dirac cohomology, since $D^2$ acts by zero there.
assumptions: On the Dirac cohomology (resp. extended Dirac index), or any submodule found inside it, namely $V_\lambda$ (resp. $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$)

nodes.name: central character element $\nu_\lambda$ of $X_\lambda$
nodes.statement:
The element $
u_\lambda$ defining the central character of $X_\lambda$ is $$
u = \sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} 
u_{\St_{\lambda_i}}.$$
assumptions: The element $\nu_\lambda$ defining the central character of $X_\lambda$

nodes.name: decomposition of $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ into spectrum eigenspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ be the genuine irreducible supermodule of $\tilde{S}_n$, associated to $\lambda$. Then the common eigenspaces for $M_i^2$ are labelled by the spectrum data $\alpha \in \Sspec(n,\lambda)$. Hence, when considered as a $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n \rangle$-supermodule, $$\tilde{\tau}_\lambda = \bigoplus_{\alpha \in \Sspec(n,\lambda)} U_\alpha.$$
nodes.statement_short: $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ decomposes over $\langle M_1,\ldots,M_n\rangle$ into eigenspaces $U_\alpha$ indexed by the spectrum data.
assumptions: Let $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ be the genuine irreducible supermodule of $\tilde{S}_n$, associated to $\lambda$
conclusions: the common eigenspaces for $M_i^2$ are labelled by the spectrum data $\alpha \in \Sspec(n,\lambda)$

nodes.name: dimension of $V_\lambda$
nodes.statement: The dimension of $V_\lambda$ is $$2^{\lceil \frac{n-l(\lambda)}{2}\rceil} \frac{n!}{\lambda_1!\ldots \lambda_r!} \Pi_{i=1}^{r} \frac{\lambda_i - \lambda_j}{\lambda_i +\lambda_j}.$$
nodes.statement_short: $\dim V_\lambda$ is the spinor dimension $2^{\lceil (n-l(\lambda))/2\rceil}$ times the number of standard shifted tableaux.
assumptions: The dimension of $V_\lambda$

nodes.name: $\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m}) = P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m}$
nodes.statement: We have $$\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m}) = P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m}.$$

nodes.name: $\underline{\zeta}$ surjects onto the even centre and kills odd polynomials
nodes.statement: The map $\underline{\zeta}$ surjects onto the even part of the centre of $\mathcal{T}_n$. Also $\ker(\underline{\zeta}) \supset S(V)_{\odd}$.
assumptions: The map $\underline{\zeta}$
conclusions: surjects onto the even part of the centre of $\mathcal{T}_n$

nodes.name: action of $\sum (2M_i)^{2m}$ for a length-one partition
nodes.statement: Fix a $t\in \mathbb{Z}$ and let $\mu = (\mu_i) = (t) \Vdash t$. Then $$\sigma_\mu(\sum_{i=1}^t (2M_i)^{2m}) = \sum_{i=1}^t (i-1)^m(i)^m.$$
assumptions: Fix a $t\in \mathbb{Z}$ and let $\mu = (\mu_i) = (t) \Vdash t$

nodes.name: $C(V)$ is supersimple with unique simple supermodule $\mathcal{S}$
nodes.statement: As an ungraded algebra the Clifford algebra $C(V)$ has, depending on $\dim(V)$, either one or two isomorphism classes of irreducible modules. However when we consider supermodules, $C(V)$ is supersimple; it always has exactly one simple supermodule, $\mathcal{S}$ \cite[12.2.4]{K05}. When $\dim(V)$ is odd then $\mathcal{S}$ is of type Q and when $\dim(V)$ is even the supermodule is of type M.
nodes.statement_short: $C(V)$ is supersimple with a unique simple supermodule $\mathcal{S}$, of type Q for odd $\dim V$ and type M for even.
assumptions: As an ungraded algebra the Clifford algebra $C(V)$ has, depending on $\dim(V)$, either one or two isomorphism classes of irreducible modules
conclusions: when we consider supermodules, $C(V)$ is supersimple; it always has exactly one simple supermodule, $\mathcal{S}$
When $\dim(V)$ is odd then $\mathcal{S}$ is of type Q and when $\dim(V)$ is even the supermodule is of type M

nodes.name: centrality of $\Omega_{\mathbb{H}}$ and its scalar action
nodes.statement:
The element $\Omega_{\mathbb{H}}$ is independent of the choice of orthonormal basis, it is central in $\mathbb{H}$ \cite[2.4]{BCT12}. Hence it acts by a scalar for any irreducible representation of $X$. Furthermore, let $(\pi,X)$ be an irreducible $\mathbb{H}$-module. It has an associated central character $\chi_
u$ which can be defined in terms of $
u \in \mathbb{H}$. It is shown in \cite[2.5]{BCT12} that $$\pi(\Omega_{\mathbb{H}})= ( 
u , 
u ).$$
nodes.statement_short: $\Omega_\mathbb{H}$ is central, hence scalar on irreducibles, and that scalar is $(\nu,\nu)$.
assumptions: let $(\pi,X)$ be an irreducible $\mathbb{H}$-module
conclusions: it acts by a scalar for any irreducible representation of $X$

nodes.name: centrality of $\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n}$
nodes.statement: The Casimir $\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n}$ is central in $\mathbb{C}[\tilde{S}_n]$, \cite{BCT12}.

nodes.name: $V_\lambda$ occurs in the Dirac cohomology of $X_\lambda$
nodes.statement: In \cite[5.8]{BCT12} it is shown that, inside the Dirac cohomology of $X_\lambda$, one can find the genuine projective irreducible representation $V_\lambda$ of isomorphism class associated to a shifted partition $\lambda \vDash n$. Since $H_D(X)$ is a quotient of $\ker(D)$, $D^2$ acts by zero on $H_D(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: $V_\lambda$ sits inside $H_D(X_\lambda)$, and $D^2$ acts by zero there.
assumptions: Since $H_D(X)$ is a quotient of $\ker(D)$
conclusions: inside the Dirac cohomology of $X_\lambda$, one can find the genuine projective irreducible representation $V_\lambda$ of isomorphism class associated to a shifted partition $\lambda \vDash n$

nodes.name: $\{\tilde{\tau}_\lambda\}$ is a transversal for the irreducible genuine projective supermodules
nodes.statement: Recall the definition of $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ \cite[A.3]{BCT12}; $$\tilde{\tau}_\lambda = \frac{1}{a_\lambda} X_{-1}(\lambda) \otimes \mathcal{S}.$$ The set $\{\tilde{\tau}_\lambda : \lambda \text{ is strict}\}$ is a transversal for the irreducible genuine projective supermodules of $S_n$.
nodes.statement_short: The $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ for strict $\lambda$ exhaust the irreducible genuine projective supermodules.
nodes.origin_citation: as recalled from [BCT12, A.3] (attributed in the introduction to [CH15, A.3])
assumptions: $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda = \frac{1}{a_\lambda} X_{-1}(\lambda) \otimes \mathcal{S}$
conclusions: The set $\{\tilde{\tau}_\lambda : \lambda \text{ is strict}\}$ is a transversal for the irreducible genuine projective supermodules of $S_n$

nodes.name: Schur's classification of the genuine projective characters
nodes.statement: Schur (cf. \cite{S89}) defined all of the genuine projective characters for $\tilde{S}_n$, and he showed that these correspond to the set of shifted partitions $\lambda \in \mathcal{SP}(n)$.
conclusions: Schur defined all of the genuine projective characters for $\tilde{S}_n$
these correspond to the set of shifted partitions $\lambda \in \mathcal{SP}(n)$

nodes.name: dimension of the ungraded representations $\tilde{\sigma}_\lambda$
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{dimension} shows that the ungraded representations $\tilde{\sigma}_\lambda$ in \cite{CH15} have dimension $$ 2^{\lfloor \frac{n-l(\lambda)}{2}\rfloor} \frac{n!}{\lambda_1!\ldots \lambda_r!} \prod_{i=1}^{r} \frac{\lambda_i - \lambda_j}{\lambda_i +\lambda_j}.$$ This is stated but not proved in \cite[Example 6.9]{CH15}.
nodes.statement_short: The ungraded $\tilde{\sigma}_\lambda$ have dimension with floor exponent, proving a formula only stated in [CH15].
assumptions: Corollary \ref{dimension}
conclusions: the ungraded representations $\tilde{\sigma}_\lambda$ in \cite{CH15} have dimension $ 2^{\lfloor \frac{n-l(\lambda)}{2}\rfloor} \frac{n!}{\lambda_1!\ldots \lambda_r!} \prod_{i=1}^{r} \frac{\lambda_i - \lambda_j}{\lambda_i +\lambda_j}$

nodes.name: sign convention for the Clifford algebra
nodes.statement: Note that this differs from some sources, \cite{BCT12} in particular, where the Clifford algebra is defined with a negative form. The theory is identical over $\mathbb{C}$ as one can just multiply the generators by $\sqrt{-1}$.

nodes.name: Morris' presentation of $W$ on all positive roots
nodes.statement: Morris also showed that one can define a presentation of $W$ with generators for each positive root \cite[3.2]{M74}, $$W = \langle z , \tilde{s}_\alpha \text{ for all } \alpha \in \Phi^+ : \tilde{s}_\alpha^2 = 1, \tilde{s}_\alpha \tilde{s}_\beta \tilde{s}_\beta = z \tilde{s}_\gamma, \gamma = s_\alpha(\beta), z^2 =1, z \text{ is central}\rangle.$$

nodes.name: root-labelled generators of $\mathcal{T}_n$ and pseudo-transpositions
nodes.statement: Following the presentation from Theorem \ref{morris} we could label the generators with the simple roots, $\alpha \in \Pi$. Then $\mathcal{T}_n$ becomes $$\langle \tau_{\alpha}, \alpha \in \Pi : (\tau_\alpha\tau_\beta)^{m(\alpha,\beta)} = (-1)^{m(\alpha,\beta) -1} \rangle.$$ Finally we also have $$\mathcal{T}_n = \langle \tau_\alpha \text{ for all } \alpha \in \Phi^+ : \tau_\alpha^2 = 1, \tau_\alpha \tau_\beta \tau_\beta = - \tau_\gamma, \gamma = s_\alpha(\beta)\rangle.$$ So by the above presentation, similarly to the symmetric group, one has for each positive root, $\alpha \in \Phi^+$, a \ `pseudo-transposition' $\tau_\alpha$. Note that this $\tau_\alpha$ is equal to the the `transposition' $[ij]$ defined in \cite[3.1]{BK01}. We will switch between labelings of the generators whenever it clarifies explanation.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{T}_n$ can be presented on root-labelled pseudo-transpositions $\tau_\alpha$, matching Brundan-Kleshchev's $[ij]$.

nodes.name: the extended Dirac index is non-zero exactly for strict partitions
nodes.statement: The extended Dirac index of $X_{-1}(\lambda)$, $I_\#(X_{-1}(\lambda))$, is non-zero if and only if $\lambda$ is strict. This follows from \cite[6.1]{CH15} and the fact that nilpotent elements that are $\delta$ quasi-distinguished have Jordan form associated to a strict partition.

nodes.name: reversing the $\textbf{q}$-grading
nodes.statement: If we let $\chi_{\textbf{q}} (\lambda)$ be the character of $X_{\textbf{q}}(\lambda)$ then $$\chi_{\textbf{q}} (\lambda ) = p^\lambda (\boldsymbol{\frac{1}{q}}) q^{n(\lambda)} $$ where $n(\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} (i-1)\lambda_i$.
nodes.statement_short: The characters of $X_{\textbf{q}}(\lambda)$ and $p^\lambda$ differ by inverting $\textbf{q}$ and shifting by $q^{n(\lambda)}$.

nodes.name: Jucys-Murphy elements anti-commute
nodes.statement: The Jucys-Murphys elements anti-commute \cite[3.1]{BK01}, that is $$M_kM_l = -M_lM_k \text{ if } k \neq l.$$

nodes.name: basis of $Z(\mathcal{T}_n)_{\even}$ from power polynomials
nodes.statement: Note that Kleschev and Brundan \cite[3.2]{BK01} provide a basis for $Z(\mathcal{T}_n)_{\even}$ in the form of products of power polynomials of the $M_i^2$. The set $\{ \Pi_{i=1}^{k} P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m_i} : \sum_{i=1}^{k}2m_i+1 \leq n\}$ is a basis for $Z(\mathcal{T}_n)_{\even}$. Therefore $$\{ \underline{\zeta}'(\Pi_{i=1}^{k} P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m_i}) : \sum_{i=1}^{k}2m_i +1 \leq n\}$$ is a basis of $Z(\mathcal{T}_n)$. For a particular $n$ it is possible to find the even elements in the kernel of $\underline{\zeta}'$ but this must be done on a case-by-case basis comparing the action on each $V_\lambda$ and showing it to be zero.
nodes.statement_short: Products of the $P^{2m}_{\mathcal{T}_n}$ form a basis of the even centre, so their $\underline{\zeta}$-preimages give a basis; kernel elements must be found case by case.

nodes.name: the symmetric group $S_n$ as a Weyl group
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be the symmetric group $S_n$. The underlying root space is $V = \Span_{\mathbb{C}} \{\xi_1,\ldots ,\xi_n\}$ and we will fix the simple roots $\Pi = \{\alpha_i =\xi_i-\xi_{i+1} : i = 1,..,n-1\},$ and positive roots $\Phi^+ = \{\xi_i-\xi_j : i <j \}$. The bilinear form is $( \xi_i , \xi_j ) = \delta_{ij}$. We have the presentation; $$S_n = \langle s_1,\ldots ,s_{n-1} : (s_is_j)^{m(i,j)} = 1 \rangle.$$ Here $m(i,i) = 1$ and $m(i,j) = -( \alpha_i , \alpha_j )( \alpha_j , \alpha_i ) +2$ if $i\neq j$ \cite{M74}. The automorphism $\delta$ come from the action of $-w_0$ on $\Phi$ hence $\delta(\alpha_i) = \alpha_{n-i}$, and $\delta(s_\alpha) = s_{\delta(\alpha)}$.
nodes.statement_short: The type-A instance: root space, simple and positive roots, Coxeter presentation of $S_n$, and $\delta(\alpha_i)=\alpha_{n-i}$.

nodes.name: the Clifford algebra $C(n)$ for $S_n$
nodes.statement: For $S_n$, the vector space $V$ has the euclidean norm and is of dimension $n$. In this case we will denote the Clifford algebra for the rank $n$ case by $C(n)$.

nodes.name: conjugate of the partition $(3,1)$
nodes.statement: If $\lambda = (3,1)$ then $\lambda' = (2,1,1)$, $$\lambda = \yng(3,1), \lambda' = \yng(2,1,1).$$

nodes.name: explicit model of $V_{(3,1)}$ for $\tilde{S}_4$
nodes.statement: Take $\tilde{S}_4$ and the shifted tableau $\lambda = (3,1) = \young(\hfil \hfil \hfil ,:\hfil ).$ There are two standard shifted tableaux, namely, $$\young(123,:4) \hspace{5mm} \young(124,:3) .$$ with content vectors $$\alpha_1 = (0,1,2,0), \alpha_2= (0,1,0,2).$$ In this case $n - l(\lambda) = 2$ so our building blocks are $C(2)$-supermodules. Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the (1,1) dimensional supermodule of $C(2) = \langle c_1 , c_2 : c_1c_2 = -c_2c_1 , c_i^2 =1\rangle$ where $$c_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 &0\end{bmatrix} \text{ and } c_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \sqrt{-1} \\ -\sqrt{-1} &0\end{bmatrix}.$$ As a superspace $V_{(3,1)} =\mathcal{S}^1 \oplus \mathcal{S}^2$, where $\mathcal{S}^j \cong \mathcal{S}$ as a $C(2)$-module. For the action of the Jucys-Murphy elements, $M_1= 0$, $M_2 = (\sqrt{2}c_1,\sqrt{2} c_1)$, $M_3 = (\sqrt{6}c_2,0)$ and $M_4 = (0,\sqrt{6}c_2)$. Finally, to calculate the action of $\tau_i$, since $s_i(\alpha_j) \in \Sspec(4, (3,1)) $ for $i = 1,2,$ then $\tau_1$ and $ \tau_2$ fix $\mathcal{S}^1$ and $\mathcal{S}^2$. Explicitly, using Definition \ref{actionoftau}: $$\tau_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \sqrt{2} & 0 & 0 \\ \sqrt{2} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} & 0 \end{bmatrix},$$ $$\tau_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{-6} - \sqrt{2}) & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{-6}+\sqrt{2}) & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$$ Now $\tau_3$ interchanges $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$, hence again using Theorem \ref{actionoftau} $$\tau_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{\sqrt{-6}}{3} & \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} & 0 \\ - \frac{\sqrt{-6}}{3} & 0 & 0 & \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \\ \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} & 0 & 0 & \frac{\sqrt{-6}}{3} \\ 0 & \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} & - \frac{\sqrt{-6}}{3} & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$$ This gives an explicit realisation of of the supermodule $V_{(3,1)}$ on the four dimensional space spanned by $\{v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\}$, by the above matrices. Although note that the even space is $V_{(3,1)}^0 = span\{v_1,v_4\}$ and the odd space is $V_{(3,1)}^1 = span\{v_2,v_3\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Worked $4$-dimensional model of $V_{(3,1)}$ for $\tilde{S}_4$: two standard shifted tableaux, $C(2)$-spinor blocks, and explicit matrices for $\tau_1,\tau_2,\tau_3$.

nodes.name: coefficients of $\nu$ for $\lambda = (5,3,2)$
nodes.statement_short: Illustrates $\nu_\lambda$ for $(5,3,2)$ by a vertically symmetric row-by-row labelling of the Young diagram.

nodes.name: specialisation $X_{-1}(e)$
nodes.statement: We can specialise $X_{\textbf{q}}(e)$ to a $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$-graded module as $$X_{-1}(e)= \sum_{i \geq 0} (-1)^{d_e - i} H^{2i}(\mathcal{B}_e) \otimes \sgn.$$

nodes.name: the element $\nu_\lambda$ defining $\chi_\lambda$
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda= (\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_k)$ be a partition. Recall the central character $\chi_\lambda$ of the $\mathbb{H}$-module $X_\lambda$ is a function $\chi_\lambda: Z(\mathbb{H}) \to \mathbb{C}$. Since $Z(\mathbb{H}) = S(V)^{S_n}$ any central character can be defined by a $S_n$ orbit of $V^*$. Let $\{y_i\}$ be a dual basis of $\{x_i\}$ then the element defining $\chi_\lambda$ is $$\nu_\lambda = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j =1}^{\lambda_i} (-\lambda_i +2j-1)y_{\lambda_{i+1}+j}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Explicit row-by-row formula for the vector $\nu_\lambda$ that defines the central character $\chi_\lambda$ of $X_\lambda$.

nodes.name: proof of the super formulation of the Dirac index
nodes.statement: From Theorem \ref{CH15prop5.10} we can describe the trace of $w \in \tilde{W}$ on $I_\#(X)$ as a product of the trace on $X$ and the difference of the trace on $\mathcal{S}^+$ and $\mathcal{S}^-$. However this is just the product of the supertrace of the modules $X$ and $\mathcal{S}$; $$ \tr(w, I_\#(X)) = \tr(p(w),X)\tr(w,S^+ - S^-) = \str(p(w),X)\str(w,S).$$
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the character identity of the cited proposition as a product of supertraces.

nodes.name: proof that the Casimirs agree on Dirac cohomology
nodes.statement: This follows from $D^2$ acting by zero and the equation given in Theorem \ref{Dirac}.
nodes.statement_short: Set $D^2 = 0$ in the Parthasarathy-type identity.

nodes.name: proof that the reduction rule removes a box from row $i$
nodes.statement: Because $\lambda$ is strict, the column of $\lambda$ which is first larger than $i$, $\lambda_{a_i}'$, will always be the column that has a block from $\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_i$ and no others. So removing a block from row $\lambda_i$ is equivalent to removing a block from column $\lambda_{a_i}'$. Hence $\lambda^{(i)} = (\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_{i-1},\lambda_{i} -1 , \lambda_{i+1},\ldots ,\lambda_r)$. The second statement follows since we have an explicit description of $\{\lambda^{(i)} : i =1,\ldots ,l(\lambda) \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Strictness forces the selected column to meet exactly rows $1,\ldots,i$, so the column removal is a row removal.

nodes.name: proof of the restriction of $X_{\textbf{q}}(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{reverse} one can write $\chi_\textbf{q}(\lambda) = p^\lambda (\boldsymbol{\frac{1}{q}}) q^{n(\lambda)}$. Then, we can use the restriction rules given by Theorem \ref{GPbranching} to restrict $\chi_\textbf{q}(\lambda)$ in terms of the characters $p^{\lambda^{(i)}}(\textbf{q})$. Remark \ref{reverse} can be used again to rewrite this in terms of characters $\chi_{\textbf{q}}(\lambda^{(i)})$. The coefficient one gets is $\textbf{q}^{i-1+ n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)})}$. Writing out the definition of $n(\lambda)$; $$n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)}) = \sum_{j=1}^l(\lambda)(j-1)\lambda_j - \sum_{j=1}^{l(\lambda^{(i)})} (j-1)\lambda^{(i)}_j.$$ However, by Lemma \ref{strictset}, $\lambda$ and $\lambda^{(i)}$ differ by only one entry for $\lambda$ strict. This difference is in the $ith$ entry. Therefore $n(\lambda)$ and $n(\lambda^{(i)})$ differ by $i-1$. Hence $i-1+ n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)}) = 2i-2$.
nodes.statement_short: Transport the Garcia-Procesi branching through the grading reversal and compute the resulting exponent $2i-2$.

nodes.name: proof of the restriction of $X_{-1}(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: This is the specialisation of Lemma \ref{qres} to $\textbf{q} = -1$.
nodes.statement_short: Specialise the graded branching rule at $\textbf{q}=-1$.

nodes.name: proof that $\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(i)}}$ occurs in the restriction
nodes.statement: We note that $a_\lambda \tilde{\tau}_\lambda = X_{-1}(\lambda) \otimes \mathcal{S}$. Here, $\mathcal{S}$ (resp. $\mathcal{S}'$) is the spinor supermodule for the Clifford algebra $C(n)$ (resp. $C(n-1)$). Hence restricting $a_\lambda \tilde{\tau_\lambda} $ to $\tilde{S}_{n-1}$ is equivalent to restricting $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ to $S_{n-1}$ and $\mathcal{S}$ to $C(n-1)$. Therefore $$a_\lambda Res^{n}_{n-1} \tilde{\tau}_\lambda = Res^{n}_{n-1}\mathcal{S} \otimes Res^{n}_{n-1} X_{-1}(\lambda) $$ $$= c \mathcal{S}' \otimes \bigoplus_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} X_{-1}(\lambda^{(i)}).$$ $$= \bigoplus_{{\lambda^{(i)}} \text{ which are strict }} c\mathcal{S}' \otimes X_{-1}(\lambda^{(i)}).$$ Here, $c \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ and will be determined in Theorem \ref{branchingrules}. Hence, for every strict $\lambda^{(i)}$ the $\tilde{S}_n$ supermodule $\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(i)}}$ occurs as a summand.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict the spinor factor and the graded factor separately, then drop the non-strict summands.

nodes.name: proof of the branching rules for $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{summands} we already know which summands will occur. Hence calculating the multiplicities is all that is required. We know the multiplicities of the restriction of the spinor $S_n$; $2$ if $n$ is even, $1$ otherwise. Also, by Lemma \ref{summands} the multiplicities in the restriction of $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ are always $1$. Hence, we can find the multiplicities for $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ by comparing $\frac{1}{a_\lambda}$ and $\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}}$ from Proposition \ref{alambda}. This is a simple calculation on the eight cases $$\frac{1}{a_\lambda} = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ 2\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}}& n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1.\\ \end{cases}$$ Note that $l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1$ occurs once if and only if $\lambda_r = 1$, in which case it is the partition $\lambda^{(r)}$ which has shorter length.
nodes.statement_short: Only multiplicities remain, and they follow from an eight-case comparison of $a_\lambda$ with $a_{\lambda^{(i)}}$.

nodes.name: proof of the action of $\Omega_\mathbb{H}$ via contents
nodes.statement: The first part can be proved by noticing that, when one forgets the grading, the module $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ is just the parabolically induced module $X_\lambda$, see \cite{BM83}. Hence, one can use Lemma \ref{HOmega} to show how $\Omega_\mathbb{H}$ acts. The constant $( \nu, \nu )$ is exactly the sum we stated. The second part follows by a simple induction. One can show $\sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_i} (2j - \lambda_i)^2= \sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_i} j(j+1) = \sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_k} q(\cont(k,j))$, splitting the cases when $\lambda_i$ is odd or even. This will be covered in more detail in Section \ref{vogan}.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ with $X_\lambda$ to get $(\nu,\nu)$, then convert the sum into contents by induction.

nodes.name: proof that $\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} = \frac{1}{2}\sum M_k^2$
nodes.statement: $$\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n}= \frac{1}{4}\sum_{\substack{\alpha,\beta\in\Phi^+ \\ s_\alpha(\beta)<0}} |\alpha||\beta|\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta $$ $$=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in \Phi^+} |\alpha||\beta|\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta= \frac{1}{4}(\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}|\alpha|\tau_\alpha)^2$$ $$=\frac{1}{4} (\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\alpha|M_k)^2= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n M_k^2$$ In the second equality, we use $\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta = - \tau_\beta \tau_{s_\alpha(\beta)}$ for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that $s_\alpha(\beta)>0$. The third equality uses the fact that every $\sum_{i=1}^n M_k = \sum_{\alpha \in \Phi^+} \tau_\alpha$ and the last equality uses the fact that the Jucys-Murphy elements anti-commute in $\mathcal{T}_n$ \cite[3.1]{BK01}. Hence the square of the sum is equal to the sum of the squares.
nodes.statement_short: Chain of four equalities: drop the $s_\alpha(\beta)<0$ condition, complete the square, rewrite in terms of $M_k$, then use anti-commutativity.

nodes.name: proof that spectrum data equals content data
nodes.statement: We prove the theorem by induction, the base case being trivial. Suppose for every shifted partition $\mu \in \mathcal{SP}(n-1)$, $\Scont(n-1, \mu) = \Sspec(n-1, \mu)$. Let us fix a shifted partition $\lambda$ of $n$, and consider $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ the irreducible representation of $\mathcal{T}_n$ associated to $\lambda$. Let $\alpha = (\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_n)\in \Sspec(n , \lambda)$. By definition there exists a vector $v_\alpha \in \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ such that $M_j^2(v_\alpha) =q(\alpha_j )v_\alpha \text{ for all } $j$.$ The restriction of $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ to $\mathcal{T}_{n-1}$ is the direct sum, $\bigoplus_{i =1}^{l(\lambda)} \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(i)}}$. Also $v_\alpha$ is an eigenvector for the Jucys-Murphys elements. Hence $v_\alpha \in \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}} \subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ for some fixed $j$. We know, by the inductive hypothesis, $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1}) \in \Sspec(n-1,\lambda^{(j)}) = \Scont(n-1,\lambda^{(j)})$. Explicitly, this means there exists a standard numbering $[[\lambda^{(j)}]]$ of $\lambda^{(j)}$ which corresponds to $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})$. Now using Lemma \ref{content}, Lemma \ref{squares} and Theorem \ref{Dirac}, we can describe the action of the Casimir elements of $\tilde{S}_n$ and $\tilde{S}_{n-1}$ on $v_\alpha$. Since $v_\alpha$ is in $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ , $$ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n M_k^2 v_\alpha = \Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} v_\alpha= \Omega_{\mathbb{H}_n}v_\alpha =\frac{1}{4} \sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \cont(i,j)(\cont(i,j)+1)v_\alpha. $$ However $v_\alpha$ is also contained in $\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}}\subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ so, $$\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} M_k^2v_\alpha = \Omega_{\tilde{S}_{n-1}} v_\alpha= \Omega_{\mathbb{H}_{n-1}}v_\alpha =\frac{1}{4} \sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda^{(j)}} \cont(i,j)(\cont(i,j)+1)v_\alpha.$$ the difference of these two Casimir elements is $\frac{1}{2}M_n^2$. Hence $$M_n^2 v_\alpha = \left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \cont(i,j)(\cont(i,j)+1) - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda^{(j)}} \cont(i,j)(\cont(i,j)+1) \right) v_\alpha$$ $$ =\frac{1}{2} \cont(k,l)(\cont(k,l)+ 1)v_\alpha,$$ where $(k,l)$ is the block of $ \lambda $ not included in $ \lambda^{(i)}.$ Taking the standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda^{(j)}]]_{(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})}$ associated to $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})$ and adding the block $(k,l)$ labelled with the number $n$ creates a standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda]]_\alpha$ of shape $\lambda$. By the above argument this standard shifted tableau has content vector equal to $\alpha \in \Sspec(n,\lambda)$. Hence $\alpha \in \Scont(n,\lambda)$. For the reverse direction, we use an almost identical argument. Suppose $\beta =(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_n) \in \Scont(n,\lambda)$ corresponds to a standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda]]_\beta$. By restriction and inductive hypothesis, there exists a vector $v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} \in \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}} \subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ such that $M_k^2 v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} = q(\beta_k) v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})}$. Again using the fact that $M_n^2$ acts by the difference of the Casimir elements $\Omega_{S_n}$ and $\Omega_{S_{n-1}}$, we get, $$M_n^2 v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} = 2(\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} - \Omega_{\tilde{S}_{n-1}}) = \frac{1}{2}q(\cont(n))v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})},$$ where $\cont(n)$ is the content of the box labelled by $n$ in $[[\lambda]]_\beta$. Hence $\beta \in Spec(n,\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$: the difference of the two Casimirs is $\frac12 M_n^2$, so the new eigenvalue is exactly the content of the added box; run the argument in both directions.

nodes.name: proof that the restriction is a sum of common eigenspaces
nodes.statement: The $M_i^2$ all commute so we can separate $V$ into its common eigenspaces. Now $M_i$ fix these spaces so the common eigenspaces are $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n \rangle$ submodules of $V$.
nodes.statement_short: The squares commute, giving a joint eigenspace decomposition preserved by the $M_i$.

nodes.name: proof that eigenspaces factor through a Clifford algebra
nodes.statement: The set of Jucys-Murphy elements anti-commute and on $U$, by Definition \ref{spec}, $M_i^2 = q(\alpha_i)$ for some $\alpha = (\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_n) \in \Sspec(n)$. By sending $M_i$ to $\frac{c_i}{\sqrt{q(\alpha_i)}}$ for $\alpha_i \neq 0$, where $c_i$ are the Clifford generators for the Clifford algebra the action of $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n \rangle$ on $U$ factors through the Clifford algebra of rank $\# \{\alpha_i \neq 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Normalise the anti-commuting $M_i$ by $\sqrt{q(\alpha_i)}$ to get Clifford generators.

nodes.name: proof that the corrected $\tau_i$ operator permutes eigenspaces
nodes.statement: One can see that for every $u \in U_\alpha$, $$M_j \left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right)u = - \left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) M_{s_i(j)}u.$$ Therefore we can conclude that $\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) U_\alpha$ is the subspace we labelled $U_{s_i(\alpha)}$. Note that if $s_i(\alpha) \notin \Sspec(n,\lambda)$ then $\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) U_\alpha = 0$ hence, in this case, $\tau_i = \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})}$ on $U_\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: The commutation relation twists $M_j$ into $M_{s_i(j)}$, identifying the image as $U_{s_i(\alpha)}$ (or zero).

nodes.name: proof that $\{V_\lambda\}$ is a full set of representatives
nodes.statement: All we need to show is that the supermodules $V_\lambda$ are isomorphic to $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$. Corollary \ref{JMsummand} shows that they are isomorphic as $\langle M_1,\ldots,M_n\rangle$-supermodules. The following arguments will show that the action of $\tau_i$ agree on both $V_\lambda$ and $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$. If $s_i(\alpha) \notin \Sspec(n,\lambda)$ then Lemma \ref{negative} shows that $\tau_i$ acts on both supermodules identically. In the case that $(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} )$ interchanges $V_\alpha$ and $S_{s_i(\alpha)}$ one observes, that applying this operator twice gives $$\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})}\right) ^2 = \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})^2})\right)Id$$ on $V_\alpha$. Let $p = 1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2} $. Furthermore, again by Lemma \ref{negative} $$\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}} P_{s_i}. $$ Rearranging this equation gives the result, $$\tau_i = \frac{M_i - M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) -q(a_{i+1})}- \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} P_{s_i} .$$ So again the action of $\tau_i$ is identical on both modules.
nodes.statement_short: Compare $V_\lambda$ with $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$: they agree over the Jucys-Murphy subalgebra, and squaring the corrected $\tau_i$ operator pins down the normalisation of $P_{s_i}$.

nodes.name: proof of the dimension of $V_\lambda$
nodes.statement: We built $V_\lambda$ as a direct sum of simple supermodules $\mathcal{S}_{n-l(\lambda)}$, which have dimension $2^{\lceil \frac{n-l(\lambda)}{2}\rceil}$. The number of $\mathcal{S}_{n-l(\lambda)}$ in the sum is equal to the number of standard shifted tableaux, which is $\frac{n!}{\lambda_1!\ldots \lambda_r!} \prod_{i=1}^{r} \frac{\lambda_i - \lambda_j}{\lambda_i +\lambda_j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the spinor dimension by the number of standard shifted tableaux.

nodes.name: proof of the criterion for $\underline{\zeta}$
nodes.statement: The set of $V_\lambda$ for shifted partitions is a full set of irreducible representations of $\mathcal{T}_n$. Also $\underline{\zeta}^*(V_\lambda) = \chi_\lambda$. So the assumption is equivalent to, for all $\sigma \in \irr(\mathcal{T}_n)$, $\sigma(P_{\mathcal{T}_n}) =(\sigma)(\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}})).$ Then applying Lemma \ref{density}, $\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}}) = P_{\mathcal{T}_n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Translate the hypothesis into agreement on all irreducibles, then apply the density lemma.

nodes.name: proof that $\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m}) = P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m}$
nodes.statement: This follows from Lemma \ref{equivalent} and Theorem \ref{action}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the criterion lemma with the matching-action theorem.

nodes.name: proof that odd power sums vanish
nodes.statement: The character $\chi_\lambda$ is defined by $\nu_\lambda$ which for every positive coefficient has a negative coefficient of the same magnitude. Hence any symmetric odd polynomial evaluated on $\nu_\lambda$ is zero.
nodes.statement_short: $\nu_\lambda$ is symmetric about zero, so odd symmetric polynomials vanish on it.

nodes.name: proof of surjectivity onto the even centre
nodes.statement: The first statement is clear since $Z(\mathcal{T})_{\even}$ is generated by the symmetric polynomials in the squares of the Jucys-Murphy elements. The second statement follows from the fact that every symmetric homogeneous polynomial of odd degree is generated by monomials of power polynomials where there is at least one odd power polynomial. Hence $\underline{\zeta}$, since it is a homomorphism, will kill any homogeneous symmetric polynomial of odd degree.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity from the generating set of the even centre; the kernel claim from factorising odd symmetric polynomials.

nodes.name: proof of the reduction to length-one partitions
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots ,\lambda_k)$ be a shifted partition. We are studying the action of power polynomials. Let $Q_{\mathbb{H}}^j$ be the $j^{th}$ power polynomial in the $x_i$'s, $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^j$. Let $\chi_{\lambda_1 \times \ldots \times \lambda_k}$ be the central character of the $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_1} \times \ldots \times \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_k}$-module $St_{\lambda_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes St_{\lambda_k}$ and $\chi_{\lambda_l}$ be the central character of the $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$-module $St_{\lambda_l}$. We consider $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$ to be embedded in $\mathbb{H}$ such that $x_{\lambda_{l-1}+1}, \ldots, x_{\lambda_l}$ are in the image of $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$. Since $Q_{\mathbb{H}}^j \in \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_1} \times \ldots \times \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_k}$, then $$\chi_\lambda(Q_\mathbb{H}^j) = \chi_{\lambda_1 \times \ldots \times \lambda_k}(Q_\mathbb{H}^j) = \sum_{l=1}^k \chi_{\lambda_l} (Q_{\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}}^j).$$ Similarly, for $Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j = \sum_{i=1}^n M_i^j$, $$\sigma_\lambda (Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j) = \sum_{l=1}^k \sigma_{\lambda_l}(Q_{\mathcal{T}_{\lambda_l}}^j).$$ Therefore if we can prove the result of the theorem for every $\mu = (\lambda_l) \in \mathcal{P}^1$, then using the above decomposition of both $\chi_\lambda(Q_\mathbb{H}^j)$ and $\sigma_\lambda (Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j)$ we can extend this to $\sigma_{\lambda}$ and $\chi_\lambda$ for every strict $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Power polynomials split along the parabolic factors on both sides, so the length-one case suffices.

nodes.name: proof of the content formula for $P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m}$
nodes.statement: This is a restatement of Theorem \ref{spectrumdata} where we described the action of $M_i^2$ on $V_\lambda$. Recall that the result showed that on a certain subspace $M_i^2$ acted by $cont(i)(cont(i)+1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Restate the spectrum-data theorem, which gives $M_i^2$ acting by $\cont(i)(\cont(i)+1)$.

nodes.name: proof of the length-one action of $\sum (2M_i)^{2m}$
nodes.statement: This follows from Lemma \ref{cont} since for $\mu$, $\cont(i) = i-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Specialise the content formula using $\cont(i)=i-1$ for a single-row shape.

nodes.name: proof of the length-one action of $\sum (2x_i)^{2m}$
nodes.statement: The central character $\chi_\mu$ is defined by $\nu_\mu = \sum_{i=1}^{t} (2(i-1) - (t-1)y_i$. The result follows by evaluating $\sum_{i=1}^t (2x_i)^{2m}$ at $\nu_\mu$.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the power sum at the explicit $\nu_\mu$.

nodes.name: proof of the matching actions for partitions of length one
nodes.statement: Fix $m \in \mathbb{N}$. We prove this statement by induction on $n$ with steps of length two. Note that for $n=0$ and $n=1$, all operators act by zero, hence the base cases are trivial. Suppose the result is true for $n-2$, so: $$\sigma_{(n-2)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \chi_{(n-2)} (P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m}).$$ Now, considering that $\sigma_{(n-2)}$ is the restriction of $\sigma_{(n)}$ to $\mathcal{T}_{n-2}$, $$\sigma_{(n)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n}}^{2m}) - \sigma_{(n-2)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \sigma_{(n)}( (2M_{n-1})^{2m} + (2M_{n})^{2m}).$$ By Corollary \ref{actionT} this is equal to \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \sum_{i=1}^{t} (i-1)^m(i)^m - \sum_{i=1}^{t-2} (i-1)^m(i)^m & = (t-2)^m(t-1)^m + (t-1)^m(t)^m\\ & = (t-1)^m ((t-1 + 1)^m + (t-1 -1 )^m ) \\ &= (t-1)^m (\sum_{l=0}^m {m\choose l} (t-1)^{m-l} (1^l + (-1)^l))\\ & = (t-1)^m\sum_{\substack{l \in {0,\ldots ,m} \\\text{ and even} }} 2 {m\choose l} (t-1)^{m-l}\\ & = \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} 2 {m \choose 2j} (t-1)^{2m-2j}. \end{split} \end{equation*} We know that $$\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}) - \chi_{(t-2)}P_{\mathbb{H}_{t-2}}^{2m},$$ is just the action of the $x_{t}$ and $x_{t-1}$. Expanding out $P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}$ and explicitly writing $\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m})$ using Lemma \ref{actionH}, we know that $$\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}) - \chi_{(t-2)}P_{\mathbb{H}_{t-2}}^{2m}= \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} 2 {m \choose 2j} (t-1)^{2m-2j}.$$ Therefore we have shown that the inductive step holds. Hence $$\sigma_{(n)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \chi_{(n)} (P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m})$$ by induction.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$ in steps of two: both sides increase by the same binomial expression $\sum_j 2\binom{m}{2j}(t-1)^{2m-2j}$.

nodes.name: strictness identifies the relevant column
nodes.statement: Because $\lambda$ is strict, the column of $\lambda$ which is first larger than $i$, $\lambda_{a_i}'$, will always be the column that has a block from $\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_i$ and no others. So removing a block from row $\lambda_i$ is equivalent to removing a block from column $\lambda_{a_i}'$. Hence $\lambda^{(i)} = (\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_{i-1},\lambda_{i} -1 , \lambda_{i+1},\ldots ,\lambda_r)$.
nodes.statement_short: Show the selected column meets exactly rows $1,\ldots,i$, so the removal happens in row $i$.

nodes.name: deduce the second statement
nodes.statement: The second statement follows since we have an explicit description of $\{\lambda^{(i)} : i =1,\ldots ,l(\lambda) \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the set equality with $\Theta^n_{n-1}(\lambda)$ from the explicit description.

nodes.name: rewrite $\chi_\textbf{q}(\lambda)$ via the grading reversal
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{reverse} one can write $\chi_\textbf{q}(\lambda) = p^\lambda (\boldsymbol{\frac{1}{q}}) q^{n(\lambda)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Express the character of $X_\textbf{q}(\lambda)$ through $p^\lambda$ with reversed grading.

nodes.name: apply the Garcia-Procesi restriction and reverse back
nodes.statement: Then, we can use the restriction rules given by Theorem \ref{GPbranching} to restrict $\chi_\textbf{q}(\lambda)$ in terms of the characters $p^{\lambda^{(i)}}(\textbf{q})$. Remark \ref{reverse} can be used again to rewrite this in terms of characters $\chi_{\textbf{q}}(\lambda^{(i)})$. The coefficient one gets is $\textbf{q}^{i-1+ n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)})}$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict with the cited branching theorem, convert back, and read off the exponent.

nodes.name: expand $n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)})$
nodes.statement: Writing out the definition of $n(\lambda)$; $$n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)}) = \sum_{j=1}^l(\lambda)(j-1)\lambda_j - \sum_{j=1}^{l(\lambda^{(i)})} (j-1)\lambda^{(i)}_j.$$
nodes.statement_short: Write the difference of the two $n$-statistics explicitly.

nodes.name: evaluate the exponent as $2i-2$
nodes.statement: However, by Lemma \ref{strictset}, $\lambda$ and $\lambda^{(i)}$ differ by only one entry for $\lambda$ strict. This difference is in the $ith$ entry. Therefore $n(\lambda)$ and $n(\lambda^{(i)})$ differ by $i-1$. Hence $i-1+ n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)}) = 2i-2$.
nodes.statement_short: Use strictness to get a difference of $i-1$, giving the exponent $2i-2$.

nodes.name: set up the spinor factorisation
nodes.statement: We note that $a_\lambda \tilde{\tau}_\lambda = X_{-1}(\lambda) \otimes \mathcal{S}$. Here, $\mathcal{S}$ (resp. $\mathcal{S}'$) is the spinor supermodule for the Clifford algebra $C(n)$ (resp. $C(n-1)$).
nodes.statement_short: Recall the tensor factorisation and name the two spinor modules.

nodes.name: restrict the two tensor factors separately
nodes.statement: Hence restricting $a_\lambda \tilde{\tau_\lambda} $ to $\tilde{S}_{n-1}$ is equivalent to restricting $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ to $S_{n-1}$ and $\mathcal{S}$ to $C(n-1)$. Therefore $$a_\lambda Res^{n}_{n-1} \tilde{\tau}_\lambda = Res^{n}_{n-1}\mathcal{S} \otimes Res^{n}_{n-1} X_{-1}(\lambda) $$ $$= c \mathcal{S}' \otimes \bigoplus_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} X_{-1}(\lambda^{(i)}).$$ $$= \bigoplus_{{\lambda^{(i)}} \text{ which are strict }} c\mathcal{S}' \otimes X_{-1}(\lambda^{(i)}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Restrict each factor, insert the known branching of $X_{-1}(\lambda)$, and drop non-strict terms.

nodes.name: conclude each strict $\lambda^{(i)}$ contributes a summand
nodes.statement: Here, $c \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ and will be determined in Theorem \ref{branchingrules}. Hence, for every strict $\lambda^{(i)}$ the $\tilde{S}_n$ supermodule $\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(i)}}$ occurs as a summand.
nodes.statement_short: Defer the constant $c$ and conclude the summand statement.

nodes.name: reduce to computing multiplicities
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{summands} we already know which summands will occur. Hence calculating the multiplicities is all that is required.
nodes.statement_short: Summands are known, so only multiplicities remain.

nodes.name: record the two known multiplicities
nodes.statement: We know the multiplicities of the restriction of the spinor $S_n$; $2$ if $n$ is even, $1$ otherwise. Also, by Lemma \ref{summands} the multiplicities in the restriction of $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ are always $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Spinor restriction contributes $2$ or $1$; the graded factor contributes $1$.

nodes.name: eight-case comparison of $a_\lambda$ and $a_{\lambda^{(i)}}$
nodes.statement: Hence, we can find the multiplicities for $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ by comparing $\frac{1}{a_\lambda}$ and $\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}}$ from Proposition \ref{alambda}. This is a simple calculation on the eight cases $$\frac{1}{a_\lambda} = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ 2\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}}& n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1.\\ \end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: Tabulate the ratio $a_\lambda / a_{\lambda^{(i)}}$ across the eight parity cases.

nodes.name: identify when the length drops
nodes.statement: Note that $l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1$ occurs once if and only if $\lambda_r = 1$, in which case it is the partition $\lambda^{(r)}$ which has shorter length.
nodes.statement_short: The length only drops when $\lambda_r=1$, explaining the exceptional last summand.

nodes.name: first part via the parabolically induced module
nodes.statement: The first part can be proved by noticing that, when one forgets the grading, the module $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ is just the parabolically induced module $X_\lambda$, see \cite{BM83}. Hence, one can use Lemma \ref{HOmega} to show how $\Omega_\mathbb{H}$ acts. The constant $( \nu, \nu )$ is exactly the sum we stated.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ with $X_\lambda$ and apply the $(\nu,\nu)$ lemma.

nodes.name: second part by induction on contents
nodes.statement: The second part follows by a simple induction. One can show $\sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_i} (2j - \lambda_i)^2= \sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_i} j(j+1) = \sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_k} q(\cont(k,j))$, splitting the cases when $\lambda_i$ is odd or even. This will be covered in more detail in Section \ref{vogan}.
nodes.statement_short: Convert the square sum into a content sum by induction, splitting on the parity of $\lambda_i$.

nodes.name: the chain of four equalities
nodes.statement: $$\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n}= \frac{1}{4}\sum_{\substack{\alpha,\beta\in\Phi^+ \\ s_\alpha(\beta)<0}} |\alpha||\beta|\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta $$ $$=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in \Phi^+} |\alpha||\beta|\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta= \frac{1}{4}(\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}|\alpha|\tau_\alpha)^2$$ $$=\frac{1}{4} (\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\alpha|M_k)^2= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n M_k^2$$
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n}$ down to $\frac12\sum M_k^2$ in four equalities.

nodes.name: justification of the second equality
nodes.statement: In the second equality, we use $\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta = - \tau_\beta \tau_{s_\alpha(\beta)}$ for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that $s_\alpha(\beta)>0$.
nodes.statement_short: The pseudo-transposition relation lets the sum run over all pairs.

nodes.name: justification of the third and last equalities
nodes.statement: The third equality uses the fact that every $\sum_{i=1}^n M_k = \sum_{\alpha \in \Phi^+} \tau_\alpha$ and the last equality uses the fact that the Jucys-Murphy elements anti-commute in $\mathcal{T}_n$ \cite[3.1]{BK01}. Hence the square of the sum is equal to the sum of the squares.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite in Jucys-Murphy elements and use anti-commutativity to expand the square.

nodes.name: set up the induction
nodes.statement: We prove the theorem by induction, the base case being trivial. Suppose for every shifted partition $\mu \in \mathcal{SP}(n-1)$, $\Scont(n-1, \mu) = \Sspec(n-1, \mu)$.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on $n$, assuming the statement at level $n-1$.

nodes.name: fix $\lambda$ and $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$
nodes.statement: Let us fix a shifted partition $\lambda$ of $n$, and consider $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ the irreducible representation of $\mathcal{T}_n$ associated to $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the shape and the corresponding irreducible.

nodes.name: take a spectrum vector and its eigenvector
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha = (\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_n)\in \Sspec(n , \lambda)$. By definition there exists a vector $v_\alpha \in \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ such that $M_j^2(v_\alpha) =q(\alpha_j )v_\alpha \text{ for all } $j$.$
nodes.statement_short: Pick $\alpha \in \Sspec(n,\lambda)$ and an associated joint eigenvector.

nodes.name: locate $v_\alpha$ in a restricted summand and apply the hypothesis
nodes.statement: The restriction of $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ to $\mathcal{T}_{n-1}$ is the direct sum, $\bigoplus_{i =1}^{l(\lambda)} \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(i)}}$. Also $v_\alpha$ is an eigenvector for the Jucys-Murphys elements. Hence $v_\alpha \in \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}} \subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ for some fixed $j$. We know, by the inductive hypothesis, $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1}) \in \Sspec(n-1,\lambda^{(j)}) = \Scont(n-1,\lambda^{(j)})$. Explicitly, this means there exists a standard numbering $[[\lambda^{(j)}]]$ of $\lambda^{(j)}$ which corresponds to $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the branching rule to place $v_\alpha$ in some $\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}}$ and get a tableau for the truncated vector.

nodes.name: compute $M_n^2$ as a difference of Casimirs
nodes.statement: Now using Lemma \ref{content}, Lemma \ref{squares} and Theorem \ref{Dirac}, we can describe the action of the Casimir elements of $\tilde{S}_n$ and $\tilde{S}_{n-1}$ on $v_\alpha$. Since $v_\alpha$ is in $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ , $$ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n M_k^2 v_\alpha = \Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} v_\alpha= \Omega_{\mathbb{H}_n}v_\alpha =\frac{1}{4} \sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \cont(i,j)(\cont(i,j)+1)v_\alpha. $$ However $v_\alpha$ is also contained in $\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}}\subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ so, $$\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} M_k^2v_\alpha = \Omega_{\tilde{S}_{n-1}} v_\alpha= \Omega_{\mathbb{H}_{n-1}}v_\alpha =\frac{1}{4} \sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda^{(j)}} \cont(i,j)(\cont(i,j)+1)v_\alpha.$$ the difference of these two Casimir elements is $\frac{1}{2}M_n^2$. Hence $$M_n^2 v_\alpha = \left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \cont(i,j)(\cont(i,j)+1) - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda^{(j)}} \cont(i,j)(\cont(i,j)+1) \right) v_\alpha$$ $$ =\frac{1}{2} \cont(k,l)(\cont(k,l)+ 1)v_\alpha,$$ where $(k,l)$ is the block of $ \lambda $ not included in $ \lambda^{(i)}.$
nodes.statement_short: Subtract the two Casimir actions to see $M_n^2$ act by the content of the extra box.

nodes.name: build the standard shifted tableau for $\alpha$
nodes.statement: Taking the standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda^{(j)}]]_{(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})}$ associated to $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})$ and adding the block $(k,l)$ labelled with the number $n$ creates a standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda]]_\alpha$ of shape $\lambda$. By the above argument this standard shifted tableau has content vector equal to $\alpha \in \Sspec(n,\lambda)$. Hence $\alpha \in \Scont(n,\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_short: Add the box labelled $n$ to get a standard shifted tableau realising $\alpha$.

nodes.name: the reverse inclusion
nodes.statement: For the reverse direction, we use an almost identical argument. Suppose $\beta =(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_n) \in \Scont(n,\lambda)$ corresponds to a standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda]]_\beta$. By restriction and inductive hypothesis, there exists a vector $v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} \in \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}} \subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ such that $M_k^2 v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} = q(\beta_k) v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})}$. Again using the fact that $M_n^2$ acts by the difference of the Casimir elements $\Omega_{S_n}$ and $\Omega_{S_{n-1}}$, we get, $$M_n^2 v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} = 2(\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} - \Omega_{\tilde{S}_{n-1}}) = \frac{1}{2}q(\cont(n))v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})},$$ where $\cont(n)$ is the content of the box labelled by $n$ in $[[\lambda]]_\beta$. Hence $\beta \in Spec(n,\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_short: Run the same Casimir-difference argument starting from a content vector to land back in the spectrum.

nodes.name: record anti-commutativity and the eigenvalues on $U$
nodes.statement: The set of Jucys-Murphy elements anti-commute and on $U$, by Definition \ref{spec}, $M_i^2 = q(\alpha_i)$ for some $\alpha = (\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_n) \in \Sspec(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: On $U$ the $M_i$ anti-commute and square to scalars $q(\alpha_i)$.

nodes.name: normalise to Clifford generators
nodes.statement: By sending $M_i$ to $\frac{c_i}{\sqrt{q(\alpha_i)}}$ for $\alpha_i \neq 0$, where $c_i$ are the Clifford generators for the Clifford algebra the action of $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n \rangle$ on $U$ factors through the Clifford algebra of rank $\# \{\alpha_i \neq 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescale the nonzero $M_i$ into Clifford generators to obtain the factorisation.

nodes.name: the twisting commutation relation
nodes.statement: One can see that for every $u \in U_\alpha$, $$M_j \left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right)u = - \left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) M_{s_i(j)}u.$$
nodes.statement_short: Commuting $M_j$ past the corrected operator replaces $j$ by $s_i(j)$ up to sign.

nodes.name: identify the image subspace
nodes.statement: Therefore we can conclude that $\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) U_\alpha$ is the subspace we labelled $U_{s_i(\alpha)}$.
nodes.statement_short: The image is exactly the $s_i(\alpha)$-eigenspace.

nodes.name: the degenerate case $s_i(\alpha)\notin\Sspec(n,\lambda)$
nodes.statement: Note that if $s_i(\alpha) \notin \Sspec(n,\lambda)$ then $\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) U_\alpha = 0$ hence, in this case, $\tau_i = \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})}$ on $U_\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: When $s_i(\alpha)$ is not spectral the operator vanishes, pinning down $\tau_i$.

nodes.name: reduce to comparing the $\tau_i$ actions
nodes.statement: All we need to show is that the supermodules $V_\lambda$ are isomorphic to $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$. Corollary \ref{JMsummand} shows that they are isomorphic as $\langle M_1,\ldots,M_n\rangle$-supermodules. The following arguments will show that the action of $\tau_i$ agree on both $V_\lambda$ and $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: The Jucys-Murphy structures already agree, so only the $\tau_i$ action needs checking.

nodes.name: the case $s_i(\alpha)\notin\Sspec(n,\lambda)$
nodes.statement: If $s_i(\alpha) \notin \Sspec(n,\lambda)$ then Lemma \ref{negative} shows that $\tau_i$ acts on both supermodules identically.
nodes.statement_short: Degenerate case handled directly by the previous lemma.

nodes.name: square the corrected operator
nodes.statement: In the case that $(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} )$ interchanges $V_\alpha$ and $S_{s_i(\alpha)}$ one observes, that applying this operator twice gives $$\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})}\right) ^2 = \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})^2})\right)Id$$ on $V_\alpha$. Let $p = 1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2} $.
nodes.statement_short: In the interchanging case the operator squares to the scalar $p$.

nodes.name: rearrange to recover the defining formula
nodes.statement: Furthermore, again by Lemma \ref{negative} $$\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}} P_{s_i}. $$ Rearranging this equation gives the result, $$\tau_i = \frac{M_i - M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) -q(a_{i+1})}- \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} P_{s_i} .$$ So again the action of $\tau_i$ is identical on both modules.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the operator with $-p^{-1/2}P_{s_i}$ and rearrange into the defining formula for $\tau_i$.

nodes.name: reformulate the hypothesis over all irreducibles
nodes.statement: The set of $V_\lambda$ for shifted partitions is a full set of irreducible representations of $\mathcal{T}_n$. Also $\underline{\zeta}^*(V_\lambda) = \chi_\lambda$. So the assumption is equivalent to, for all $\sigma \in \irr(\mathcal{T}_n)$, $\sigma(P_{\mathcal{T}_n}) =(\sigma)(\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}})).$
nodes.statement_short: Restate the hypothesis as agreement of two central elements on every irreducible.

nodes.name: apply the density lemma
nodes.statement: Then applying Lemma \ref{density}, $\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}}) = P_{\mathcal{T}_n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude equality by the density lemma.

nodes.name: surjectivity onto the even centre
nodes.statement: The first statement is clear since $Z(\mathcal{T})_{\even}$ is generated by the symmetric polynomials in the squares of the Jucys-Murphy elements.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity follows from the generating set of the even centre.

nodes.name: odd symmetric polynomials lie in the kernel
nodes.statement: The second statement follows from the fact that every symmetric homogeneous polynomial of odd degree is generated by monomials of power polynomials where there is at least one odd power polynomial. Hence $\underline{\zeta}$, since it is a homomorphism, will kill any homogeneous symmetric polynomial of odd degree.
nodes.statement_short: Odd symmetric polynomials always contain an odd power sum factor, which is killed.

nodes.name: set up power polynomials and parabolic factors
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots ,\lambda_k)$ be a shifted partition. We are studying the action of power polynomials. Let $Q_{\mathbb{H}}^j$ be the $j^{th}$ power polynomial in the $x_i$'s, $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^j$. Let $\chi_{\lambda_1 \times \ldots \times \lambda_k}$ be the central character of the $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_1} \times \ldots \times \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_k}$-module $St_{\lambda_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes St_{\lambda_k}$ and $\chi_{\lambda_l}$ be the central character of the $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$-module $St_{\lambda_l}$. We consider $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$ to be embedded in $\mathbb{H}$ such that $x_{\lambda_{l-1}+1}, \ldots, x_{\lambda_l}$ are in the image of $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the power polynomials and the central characters of the parabolic factors.

nodes.name: both sides split over the factors
nodes.statement: Since $Q_{\mathbb{H}}^j \in \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_1} \times \ldots \times \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_k}$, then $$\chi_\lambda(Q_\mathbb{H}^j) = \chi_{\lambda_1 \times \ldots \times \lambda_k}(Q_\mathbb{H}^j) = \sum_{l=1}^k \chi_{\lambda_l} (Q_{\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}}^j).$$ Similarly, for $Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j = \sum_{i=1}^n M_i^j$, $$\sigma_\lambda (Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j) = \sum_{l=1}^k \sigma_{\lambda_l}(Q_{\mathcal{T}_{\lambda_l}}^j).$$
nodes.statement_short: Both the Hecke and twisted-algebra power sums decompose along the parts of $\lambda$.

nodes.name: conclude the reduction
nodes.statement: Therefore if we can prove the result of the theorem for every $\mu = (\lambda_l) \in \mathcal{P}^1$, then using the above decomposition of both $\chi_\lambda(Q_\mathbb{H}^j)$ and $\sigma_\lambda (Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j)$ we can extend this to $\sigma_{\lambda}$ and $\chi_\lambda$ for every strict $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: The length-one case therefore implies the general case.

nodes.name: set up induction in steps of two with trivial base cases
nodes.statement: Fix $m \in \mathbb{N}$. We prove this statement by induction on $n$ with steps of length two. Note that for $n=0$ and $n=1$, all operators act by zero, hence the base cases are trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on $n$ two at a time; $n=0,1$ are trivial.

nodes.name: inductive hypothesis at $n-2$
nodes.statement: Suppose the result is true for $n-2$, so: $$\sigma_{(n-2)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \chi_{(n-2)} (P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Assume the identity for $n-2$.

nodes.name: isolate the two new terms
nodes.statement: Now, considering that $\sigma_{(n-2)}$ is the restriction of $\sigma_{(n)}$ to $\mathcal{T}_{n-2}$, $$\sigma_{(n)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n}}^{2m}) - \sigma_{(n-2)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \sigma_{(n)}( (2M_{n-1})^{2m} + (2M_{n})^{2m}).$$
nodes.statement_short: The increment on the $\mathcal{T}_n$ side is the contribution of $M_{n-1}$ and $M_n$.

nodes.name: evaluate the increment by a binomial computation
nodes.statement: By Corollary \ref{actionT} this is equal to \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \sum_{i=1}^{t} (i-1)^m(i)^m - \sum_{i=1}^{t-2} (i-1)^m(i)^m & = (t-2)^m(t-1)^m + (t-1)^m(t)^m\\ & = (t-1)^m ((t-1 + 1)^m + (t-1 -1 )^m ) \\ &= (t-1)^m (\sum_{l=0}^m {m\choose l} (t-1)^{m-l} (1^l + (-1)^l))\\ & = (t-1)^m\sum_{\substack{l \in {0,\ldots ,m} \\\text{ and even} }} 2 {m\choose l} (t-1)^{m-l}\\ & = \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} 2 {m \choose 2j} (t-1)^{2m-2j}. \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand binomially; odd terms cancel, leaving $\sum_j 2\binom{m}{2j}(t-1)^{2m-2j}$.

nodes.name: the same increment on the Hecke side
nodes.statement: We know that $$\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}) - \chi_{(t-2)}P_{\mathbb{H}_{t-2}}^{2m},$$ is just the action of the $x_{t}$ and $x_{t-1}$. Expanding out $P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}$ and explicitly writing $\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m})$ using Lemma \ref{actionH}, we know that $$\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}) - \chi_{(t-2)}P_{\mathbb{H}_{t-2}}^{2m}= \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} 2 {m \choose 2j} (t-1)^{2m-2j}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Compute the corresponding increment for $\chi$ and get the same expression.

nodes.name: close the induction
nodes.statement: Therefore we have shown that the inductive step holds. Hence $$\sigma_{(n)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \chi_{(n)} (P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m})$$ by induction.
nodes.statement_short: Equal increments plus equal base cases give the result.
